meta.title: Urdu B2 Upper Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Urdu → English (see the Urdu, recall the meaning) and English → Urdu (see an English meaning, recall the Urdu). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1500 words for an upper-intermediate learner, aligned to B2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main ideas of complex text on both concrete and abstract topics, including technical discussions in their field of specialisation' — a learner here is able to interact with a degree of fluency and spontaneity that makes regular interaction with native speakers quite possible without strain for either party, and to produce clear, detailed text on a wide range of subjects and explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Urdu, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 22 of the 1500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — politics and public administration, the law and the courts, the economy and finance, science and research, technology, the environment and natural resources, health and the mind, the arts, literature and the media, history and society, argument and evaluation — the words for claims, evidence, causes and consequences — the formal connectors of written Urdu, and the verbs of reporting, analysing and persuading — and the other 1478 are the commonest remaining words of Urdu, by two frequency lists averaged, one built from film and television subtitles and one from written Urdu (Wikipedia, the web and social media), each counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first; because half the count is written Urdu, the news's words (government, minister, court) come earlier than a phrase book would put them. Every headword is printed in the Urdu script, right to left and without the short-vowel marks, as Urdu is written, with a romanisation beneath it, Wiktionary's own (ā ī ū for the long vowels, a tilde for nasalisation: khānā, ma͠i), which shows the vowels the script leaves out; the Urdu Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the script itself. The 1103 nouns show their gender, masculine or feminine, which every adjective, postposition and past-tense verb agrees with, and their plural; the 46 verbs show their past forms, where Urdu verbs are irregular, and behind the All forms fold their key forms and their tenses. Real example sentences come with 100 of the 1500 words, three apiece for 8 of them (Tatoeba has only a few thousand Urdu sentences), with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword (whether it speaks depends on an Urdu voice being installed on your device). Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, forms and romanisation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0) and the wordfreq project's Urdu list (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
